abstract: Protein structure dictates function and proteins often perform the same function in different cell or tissue-type. Here, we report that in Drosophila melanogaster, the broadly expressed protein Ref(2)P, an orthologue of mammalian p62/SQSTM1, performs mutually exclusive functions across tissues - autophagy in midgut and mitochondria-associated proteostasis in muscle. These functional differences arise from tissue-specific secondary and tertiary structures adopted by the same Ref(2)P polypeptide, rather than protein abundance, isoforms, post-translational modification, or binding-partner availability. The tissue-specific structures are cell autonomous and resistant to environmental perturbation. Deletion of a short intrinsically disordered region converts muscle Ref(2)P to a midgut-like structural and functional state. However, this forced switch causes muscle dysfunction, linking tissue-specific physiology to alternative structural states of the same polypeptide. We posit that Drosophila Ref(2)P exemplifies a mechanism for tissue-specificity, protein pleomorphism, in which the intrinsic structural plasticity of a protein and the physicochemical/molecular environment of a tissue enable a broadly expressed protein to adopt tissue-specific structure and function.
